title: Yayati's thousand years
hookLine: a king borrows his son's youth for a thousand years and learns why, to the discerning, even pleasure holds pain
carry: duhkha: feeding desire never puts it out
tomorrow: a born hermit is sent to learn freedom from a king. why a king?

cards: King Yayati is cursed with sudden old age. His father-in-law, the sage Shukra, leaves one way out: if a son will take the old age, Yayati can have that son's youth. Four sons refuse.
The youngest, Puru, says yes. So Yayati is young again, and the Mahabharata says he enjoys it for a thousand years. Every pleasure a king could want.
At the end of it, he calls Puru back.

teach.h: FIRE FED WITH GHEE ONLY GROWS.
teach.b: He gives the youth back, and says the line Hindus still quote: desire is never quenched by enjoying what's desired. Like fire fed with ghee, it only grows. Then he goes to the forest.
A thousand years, and it wasn't enough, because enough was never coming.

teach.h: 2.15: TO THE DISCERNING, ALL IS SUFFERING.
teach.b: Now Patanjali, sutra 2.15: to the discerning, all is duhkha, suffering. It sounds gloomy. It's a diagnosis, and Yayati is the case.
Patanjali gives four reasons even pleasure hides pain. Change: the sweet thing is already ending, like borrowed youth. Anxiety: while you have it, you fear losing it.
Impressions: each pleasure leaves a groove that wants more, the ghee on the fire. And the three qualities of nature, always pulling against each other.
The commentary says most people are like an arm: a thread of wool lands and nothing is felt. The discerning are like the eye, and the same thread hurts.

teach.h: AVOID THE PAIN NOT YET COME.
teach.b: Then the turn, 2.16: heyam duhkham anagatam, the suffering not yet come is to be avoided.

teach.h: FEEDING DESIRE NEVER PUTS IT OUT.
teach.b: And 2.17 names the cause: the seer joined to the seen.
Hindus who fast, on Ekadashi, in Navratri, on a weekday for a chosen god, do it first as devotion; many teachers add Yayati's reason: going without a little, on purpose, keeps the fire from growing.
Today it's the next order, the next episode, the next scroll. Yayati already ran that experiment, for a thousand years.

how: Yayati's verse about fire and ghee is quoted across Hindu texts, including the Bhagavata Purana and the Manusmriti. Many Hindus keep fasts such as Ekadashi as devotion and as practice in going without, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present 2.15–2.17 as a medical outline: the illness and its cause, with the cure and remedy to follow.

o: a feeling that only weak people have
a gloomy mood that the wise should hide
suffering: the unease the discerning can feel

games.q: the king and the sutras — tap the pairs.
p: a thousand years of youth, still not enough
feels the thread other limbs ignore
avoid the pain not yet come

s: Yayati said enjoying what you want never quenches desire
like fire fed with ghee, it only grows. then he gave the youth back.
Patanjali says life is miserable for everyone
the line says to the discerning: the one sensitive enough, like an eyeball, to feel what others miss.
the sutras blame the world itself for suffering
2.17 names the cause as the joining of the seer and the seen, not the world.

games.q: after a thousand years of every pleasure, Yayati says desire grows like fire fed with ghee. which reason in 2.15 is that?
o: impressions: each pleasure leaves a groove that wants more.
none: the pleasures were just too small.
games.why: samskara, the groove pleasure leaves. feeding it only grows it, so 2.16 turns to the pain not yet come.

practice: Bring to mind one small want that keeps coming back, a snack, a scroll, one more episode. Feel it rise, like a flame. This once, don't feed it.

Watch what the flame does when no ghee comes: it flares, then often settles. If you pray, offer that want to God the way a fasting family offers the day. If you don't, just let it be a small, chosen going-without.

wordCard.voice: Duhkha, suffering, pain, unease, the opposite of sukha, ease. Not a mood but a sensitivity, like the eye that feels the thread, and a turn toward the pain that hasn't come yet.

orig.note: Sanskrit duḥkha: pain, suffering, unease; the opposite of sukha, ease.

carryVoice: Your line: duhkha, feeding desire never puts it out. Yayati took a thousand years to learn it. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Yayati's curse of old age; Puru takes it; a thousand years; 'desire is never quenched by enjoyment; like fire fed with ghee it grows')
Bhagavata Purana 9.18–9.19 (Yayati and Puru; the same verse)
Yoga Sutra 2.15 (to the discerning, all is suffering, for four reasons)
Yoga Sutra 2.16 (the suffering not yet come is to be avoided)
Yoga Sutra 2.17 (the cause: the conjunction of seer and seen)
Yoga Bhashya on 2.15 (the eyeball and the thread of wool; the fourfold outline like medicine)
